Subject: Before we get busier

Dear Mehak,

I keep thinking about Ronit's company. Two friends, no paperwork, and when they split, each side had a different memory of who owned what. Now they don't speak. Another founder I know tells the same story. Nothing was wrong with any of them when they started. That's what bothers me.

We get along well today, so this is the right time to sort out the boring parts: how our shares vest over time, and how one of us can buy the other out fairly if we ever part. I'd like us to write both down and have a lawyer read them before we sign.

I hope this doesn't sound like I expect us to fail. It's because I want us to stay friends whatever happens.

Nandini

Harish, most founders don't want to talk about breaking up on day one. It feels like planning a divorce at the wedding. I'm Anand, and my co-founder and I did it anyway, and I'm glad. We had both watched friends' startups fall apart: one ended in a legal notice, one where the founder who left after six months kept half the company.
So in our first month, while we still liked each other a lot, we sat with a startup lawyer and agreed on the basics. Shares would vest over four years, so you earn them by staying. And if one of us left, there was a fixed way to value the shares and buy them back.
Two years later, my co-founder did leave, for family reasons. It was sad. But nobody had to argue. We just opened the document and followed it.

How did Anand feel when the co-founder left?
qa.a: Anand felt sad, but relieved that nobody had to argue because the rules were already set.

qa.q: What made agreeing the terms in the first month a wise choice?
qa.a: They were still friendly and calm, so the rules were fair to both instead of being fought over during a split.

qa.q: What would have changed if they had waited until the co-founder left?
qa.a: They would have had to agree terms while sad and possibly resentful, which could have ended in a legal notice like their friends'.

grounding: It shows co-founders who had seen other startups split badly setting vesting and a buyout method while still friendly, so a later exit follows calm rules.

Charu and her co-founder Farah were the happiest pair I knew, which is why the scene in their office surprised me. I had dropped in with samosas one evening and found them on a video call with a startup lawyer, going through a document titled "If we split".
Charu explained it to me afterwards, very matter-of-fact. "Two of my friends' companies ended in court. Both times, they tried to agree what was fair after they already hated each other." So she and Farah were setting it now: shares earned over four years, and a written way to value and buy out anyone who left.
Farah joked that it felt like writing a will. Charu didn't laugh; she just said, "Better now, while we'd both be fair."
I can't say whether it was comfortable for them. But they signed it that night and went back to arguing happily about logos.
— Swati

qa.q: Why is setting the terms while friendly a wise move?
qa.a: Both are more likely to be fair now, instead of fighting over what is fair after trust has broken.
